In the CRT group, anticoagulation strategies were recorded, including dose adjustments for liver/kidney dysfunction [ ] ; anticoagulants were categorized as LMWH alone, LMWH bridged with rivaroxaban, or no anticoagulation, with hospitalization duration of anticoagulation (days) and pre-discharge DUS results documented. 2.3. Laboratory and ultrasound assessments Pre-insertion baseline laboratory values, including complete blood count and toxin-specific analyses, were collected. Sonologist performed DUS evaluated thrombus status in the distal external iliac, common femoral, and distal deep veins, classified into: complete recanalization (no thrombus; partial recanalization) thrombus size reduced ≥ 50% or stable; thrombosis progression: enlarged thrombus or new adjacent DVT. Two DUS results were collected, including the 1st examination around the time of catheter removal and the last examination before hospital discharge; PE suspicion prompted computed tomography angiography. 2.4. Statistical analysis Statistical analysis was performed using Statistic Package for Social Science 26.0 (International Business Machines Corporation, Armonk ). Statistical significance was defined as P < .05. Continuous variables with normal distribution were reported as mean ± standard deviation, while those with skewed distribution use median (interquartile range). Student t test or the Mann–Whitney rank sum test according to the normality of their distribution. Categorical variables were expressed as frequency and percentage. Categorical variables were compared using the χ 2 test (or Fisher exact test for variables with an expected value of < 5). Significant variables in the hypothesis testing were entered into a multivariate logistic regression model to identify independent predictors. Goodness-of-fit of the regression model was examined with the Hosmer–Lemeshow test, of which P < .05 was considered statistically significant. Associations were expressed as OR with 95% CI. 3. Results 3.1. Patient characteristics After reviewing the medical records of discharged patients, of 171 patients who received ECTRs for poisoning, 71 met the inclusion criteria (Fig. ). Of patients that received a DUS, 38% had CRT. As can be seen in Table , there were no significant differences in most demographic characteristics and laboratory test results between patients with (n = 27) or without (n = 44) CRT. However, fibrinogen (3.23 (IQR = 0.83) g/L) and D-dimer (1.16 (IQR = 1.61) mg/L) concentrations were significantly higher in the CRT group ( P < .001). Also, the positive rate of D-dimer (n = 20 (74.1%)) was much higher in the CRT group ( P < .001). 3.2. Types of poisons Details of the types of poisons in the 2 groups of patients are shown in Table . Regarding the relative frequenices of the poison types, no significant differences were found between the 2 groups ( P > .05). 3.3. Clinical data The clinical data of the 2 groups of patients are shown in Table . There was no significant difference in femoral venous catheterization side ( P = .477), indwelling catheter time ( P = .140), total time of ECTRs ( P = .962), or catheter dysfunction ( P = .349) between the 2 groups. But the incidence of local symptoms was significantly higher in the CRT group ( P < 0.001). No puncture site infections occurred in either group. In terms of complications, although the incidence of progressive lower extremity DVT was higher in the CRT group ( P = .051), no major bleeding events or typical PE symptoms were observed in either group, including shortness of breath, chest pain, hemoptysis, jugular vein filling, or hypotension. No deaths were directly caused by catheter removal or its complications. 3.4. Statistical analysis for indicators of the CRT group In the multivariate logistic regression model (Table ), independent indicators of poisoned patients included positive D-dimer ( P = .002) and local symptoms ( P = .002). The Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test indicated a good model fit ( P = .540). No cases of PE were observed across any thrombus outcome category. Since this study excluded patients who received anticoagulant therapy for CRT between the end of ECTR and catheter removal, the anticoagulant therapies analyzed in the results were all interventions administered for CRT after catheter removal. The distribution of anticoagulants was as follows: LMWH in 17/27 (63.0%) patients, LMWH bridged with rivaroxaban in 6/27 (22.2%) patients, and no anticoagulation in 4/27 (14.8%) patients. Some poisoned patients had abnormal liver and kidney function in the early stages, but all improved after ECTRs. The doses of anticoagulant treatment were all determined according to the usual anticoagulation standards. In the CRT group, 4/27 (14.8%) patients did not receive anticoagulation therapy, 17/27 (63.0%) patients received anticoagulation therapy for 1 to 10 days (5.53 ± 2.94 days), and 6/27 (22.2%) patients received anticoagulation therapy for 11 to 35 days (22.17 ± 7.99 days). None of the discharged patients experienced progression of CRT to extensive DVT after discontinuing anticoagulation. 4. Discussion This retrospective study compared poisoned patients with femoral venous catheters for ECTR, identifying 2 key findings in CRT versus non-CRT groups. First, CRT did not pose immediate life-threatening risk during short-term removal: DUS showed high post-removal thrombus recanalization, supporting safe immediate removal without delay. These outcomes suggest CRT alone does not require delayed removal in acute poisoning. Second, elevated fibrinogen, positive D-dimer, and local puncture-site symptoms correlated with higher CRT risk, indicating targeted screening via lower extremity venous ultrasonography to monitor progression. Poisoning is a unique clinical condition marked by rapid progression, multisystem toxin effects, internal environment disruption, and the need for time-critical ECTRs: both short-term interventions. While some toxins affect coagulation, the direct link between specific toxins and thrombosis remains unclear. Prior research has associated long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide (warfarin) poisoning with thrombosis, hypothesized to result from early depletion of anticoagulant proteins C and S, [ ] which may exacerbate preexisting thrombophilia. Animal toxins like snake venom and carbon monoxide poisoning can also induce coagulation disorders or hypercoagulable states. [ , ] This study focused on the systemic impacts of poisoning and treatment characteristics rather than single-toxin effects, classifying poison types to ensure group comparability. By comparing the incidence of thrombus-related complications between the 2 groups, we found that there was no significant difference between the 2 groups in terms of PE, DVT, or bleeding. Some studies have shown that the embolic potential of CRT does not seem to be high in cancer patients [ , ] and is lower than that of DVT of the lower extremities. [ ] Another study noted that CRT was a benign and inevitable event that occurred after vascular wall trauma, and asymptomatic CRT usually did not require treatment. [ ] In another retrospective study based on peripherally inserted central catheters, J. Shatzel et al determined the rates of progressive thrombosis and bleeding in cohorts of patients who underwent catheter removal versus those who had catheters removed and received anticoagulation, and they thought that catheter removal alone may be an option for CRT. [ ] Therefore, since the current recommendation is based on the extrapolation of lower extremity thrombosis data, many researchers believe that direct removal of the catheter is a reasonable treatment option. Among the 71 included patients, no PE or fatal thromboembolic events were observed during or after catheter removal. In this study, 96.3% of CRT showed no progression. The condition of poisoning usually improves after ECTR. Additionally, the duration of ECTRs and catheter indwelling time were relatively short. These factors may contribute to the low risk of PE observed. Based on the data in this study, we found that CRT did not pose immediate life-threatening risk during short-term removal, so we supposed that CRT alone does not require delayed removal in acute poisoning. [ , ] Thus, lower extremity venous ultrasonography is recommended before removal in poisoned patients with temporary ECTR and elevated these biomarkers, though factors like kidney disease or infection may influence results. A significant between-group difference in local symptoms ( P < .001) was noted, with puncture-site pain a common CRT sign. [ , ] However, pain can also arise from the catheter insertion procedure itself, making it challenging to determine whether pain precedes or results from thrombosis in this context. Current guidelines recommend proactive DUS examination for patients with suspected CRT presenting with local symptoms or signs. [ ] Regression analysis in this study identified positive D-dimer results and local symptoms as key predictors of CRT. Clinically, these characteristics can help identify poisoned patients undergoing ECTR who are at high risk for this condition. For such high-risk individuals, DUS evaluation of the lower extremity veins is advised before catheter removal to inform safe management decisions. In terms of data collection, complete pre-removal DUS data were not available for all patients, and potential mobilization of catheter-related thrombi during removal might have been undetected. In the CRT group, 5 of 27 patients underwent pre-removal lower extremity venous DUS, compared with 14 of 44 patients in the non-CRT group. For general patients, omitting pre-removal lower extremity venous DUS does not contradict established treatment principles. [ ] Central venous catheter-associated thrombosis can be classified into 4 types: fibrin sheath, intraluminal clot, mural thrombosis, and venous thrombosis. [ ] Notably, the fibrin sheath differs from true thrombotic processes in etiology, pathophysiology, and clinical course, [ ] and no clear association exists between intraluminal clots and venous thrombosis. Review of DUS results in the CRT group revealed that 25 of 27 patients had mural thrombosis, and 2 had venous thrombosis. Among the 5 pre-removal DUS examinations, the other 2 thrombosis types were not identified. However, the inherent limitations of retrospective analysis, such as incomplete imaging data, should be acknowledged. Among 22.2% (6/27) patients in the CRT group exhibited catheter dysfunction, 2 patients were diagnosed with complete femoral vein occlusion caused by venous thrombosis before catheter removal, and the other 4 patients were diagnosed with local mural thrombus after catheter removal. We cannot further determine whether the catheter failure was caused by mural thrombus. The type of CRT should be clear by DUS before catheter removal. Prospective studies are needed to explore the relationship between the amount of thrombus and catheter function. Compared with traditional central venous catheters used for infusion, ECTR catheters are associated with greater blood flow velocity, the formation of a turbulent flow area outside the tip of the catheter and stimulating thrombosis. [ , ] At present, it is believed that reducing the indwelling catheter time and use can prevent CRT. [ ] Catheter dysfunction is often secondary to thrombotic occlusion or fibrin sheath formation after a catheter has previously functioned adequately. [ ] Although there was no significant difference in these 3 aspects, time of indwelling catheter and ECTRs, catheter dysfunction, between the 2 groups of patients in this study, this might be due to the small sample size. Currently, there are no established guidelines for selecting anticoagulation strategies in poisoned patients with CRT, primarily because of the limited patient population in this specific clinical context. In this study, patients underwent DUS examinations and D-dimer concentration before discharge. For those who showed thrombus resolution or reduced D-dimer concentration, the risk of venous thromboembolism was considered decreased, and preventive measures were implemented, including patient education, regular physical activity, and venous function-protective medications (such as Aescuven forte or Diosmin tablets). Anticoagulation therapy in this study cohort was limited to LMWH or a combination of LMWH and rivaroxaban, with no serious treatment-related complications observed. Although some studies propose using anticoagulants to stabilize thrombi before catheter removal, [ , , ] this approach lacks empirical validation in the existing literature. The duration of anticoagulation in this study was intentionally shortened, taking into account factors such as the unclear long-term benefit-risk profile of such therapy in poisoned patients and the resolution of acute poisoning and ECTR-related risks. No patients discontinued anticoagulation therapy due to adverse drug reactions. Whether the anticoagulation duration for this patient population should align with the guidelines for deep vein thrombosis remains undefined and requires additional research. In addition, 14.8% (4/27) patients did not receive anticoagulants, and the thrombus morphology did not change. They were not diagnosed with PE. For poisoned patients with CRT, not receiving anticoagulants may also be safe. However, anticoagulant therapy was not the aim of this study. Due to the retrospective nature, small sample size, and doctor preferences in this study, additional analyses on anticoagulation therapy in these patients were not possible. Prospective studies are expected to address these issues in the future. This study has limitations. As a retrospective study, there is a selection bias. The sample size is small, which may affect the reliability of statistical analysis results. Many eligible patients were excluded due to the lack of DUS or laboratory test results. In the clinical evaluation and treatment of CRT, different doctors may have different opinions. In addition, this study only included patients who underwent ECTRs through the femoral vein in a single center. 5. Conclusion In this small cohort of poisoned patients with short-term ECTRs, CRT does not pose immediate life-threatening risks for femoral venous catheter removal, justifying safe and timely removal. Elevated fibrinogen, positive D-dimer, and local puncture-site symptoms indicate increased thrombosis risk. Prospective studies are needed to validate these findings and refine management strategies. chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Derived from willow bark ( Salix alba ), topical salicylates are used for both pain and dermatologic concerns. They are found in many common over-the-counter (OTC) products including aspirin, bismuth subsalicylate, and oil of wintergreen. When salicylates are applied to the skin, they work by acidifying the stratum corneum, promoting the desquamation of corneocytes, and reducing intercellular cohesion. This disruption weakens the skin’s barrier properties and facilitates topical absorption. Topical salicylates are available in a variety of formulations, including patches, gels, and creams, with concentrations ranging from 0.5% for cosmetic purposes to 50% for treating conditions such as warts. Many of these OTC products are heavily advertised by famous, former pro athletes without any risk discussion. Despite their widespread use, topical salicylates can be absorbed enough to cause systemic toxicity particularly when a large dose of high concentration (milligrams per milliliter [mg/mL]) salicylates are applied to large body surface areas (amount applied) or with repeated applications (frequency). Individuals with risk factors such as decreased renal function or compromised skin integrity are at greater risk. However, toxicity can also occur in individuals without traditional risk factors highlighting the need for greater public education and clinical awareness about topical salicylate products. The condition of the skin, the concentration of the salicylate product, the vehicle/diluent used in the product, the frequency of application, and the surface area applied are all important variables that determine topical dosing and the potential for toxicity. A recent case of an elderly male with altered mental status secondary to topical salicylate toxicity emphasizes that this remains a potential source of salicylate toxicity. The patient’s presentation demonstrates the potential for significant systemic absorption even in the absence of well-known risk factors such as damaged skin or significant renal impairment. Additionally, we review previously published case reports of topical salicylate toxicity to emphasize associated risks and the importance of early recognition, intervention, and prevention of misuse particularly in high-risk populations such as pediatric and elderly demographics. The dermal route of salicylates absorption, although rare, remains a clinical problem seen in the emergency department (ED). CASE REPORT A 78-year-old male with achalasia type II, advanced dementia, alcoholic cirrhosis complicated by gastric varices, chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, traumatic brain injury, and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation presented to the ED because of altered mental status over the prior three days. His family was concerned that he was less communicative and had a loss of appetite. He denied any symptoms of dizziness, lightheadedness, tinnitus, nausea, or vomiting. His medications included 12.5 mg of trazodone at night and 15 mL of lactulose twice daily. After a review of the chart and interviewing the family, there were no oral medications containing any formulations of salicylate in the household. Initial vital signs included a blood pressure of 107/64 millimeters of mercury (mm Hg), heart rate of 85 beats per minute, and respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute with an oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. The oral temperature was recorded as 36.9°C. The skin exam did not reveal any signs of lotions, patches, acute trauma, rashes, or infection. A basic metabolic panel revealed a creatinine of 1.02 mg per deciliter (mg/dL) similar to his prior values. Other initial lab work was notable for an elevated anion gap of 16 (sodium 141 millimoles (mmol) per dL; chloride 103 mmol/dL; carbon dioxide 22 mmol/dL; and potassium 4.0 mmol/dL); and a slightly elevated venous serum pH of 7.45. A comprehensive blood panel included a white blood cell count of 3.8 thousand cells per microliter (cells/μL), hemoglobin of 11.0 grams per dL (g/dL) and platelet count of 140 thousand cells/μL. Urinalysis found moderate bacteria, trace leukocyte esterase and trace ketones. An arterial blood gas found a partial pressure of oxygen of 100 mm Hg, 94% saturated, a partial pressure of carbon dioxide of 31 mm Hg, and a pH of 7.54 consistent with a respiratory alkalosis/alkalemia with mild hyperventilation. Imaging results, including a computed tomography of the head without contrast and a chest radiograph, were both unremarkable for any acute findings. In evaluating the cause of his change in mental status and elevated anion gap, a serum salicylate level was drawn. The serum salicylate level was elevated to 41.4 mg/dL. His ethanol and acetaminophen levels were undetectable. The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for close monitoring of symptoms, and frequent repeat serum salicylate levels, blood gases, and electrolyte values. Additional potassium was given to maintain the serum level ≥ 4 mmol/dL Although the patient denied symptoms of a urinary tract infection, given his urinalysis findings and altered mental state, he was empirically treated with antibiotics. The sodium bicarbonate infusion ran ≈ 12 hours and was stopped when the serum salicylate decreased below 30 mg/dL. The anion gap returned to normal. While the family was adamant that the only salicylates to which the patient had access were the topical products, we could not completely rule out additional oral or chronic poisoning. The patient was discharged after two days of hospitalization at his baseline mental status and with the last measured serum salicylate level of 27.0 mg/dL. summarizes the serum salicylate levels in this patient. METHODS We performed a systematic and comprehensive review of cases of topical salicylate toxicity. A literature search using PubMed, Google, and Google Scholar identified relevant publications from 1952–2024. The search strategy employed the following combinations of terms: “topical salicylate toxicity,” “poisoning,” “salicylate,” “methyl salicylate,” and “case reports.” The search resulted in all available publications and specifically targeted peer-reviewed case reports, case series, conference abstracts, reviews, and letters to the editor. It also included texts found in Dutch, English, French, German, Italian, Polish, and Turkish. We used two previous literature reviews on topical salicylate toxicity published prior to our study to ensure all the papers were included. The first, by Brubacher and Hoffman in 1996, reviewed 17 cases. A subsequent review by Madan and Levitt in 2014 expanded the dataset to include 25 cases but did not include all the cases in the first review. The case data extractions were done by all the authors. Some published literature was available only in abstract form. In those cases, we extracted all relevant information provided, such as the highest plasma salicylate concentrations and patient symptoms. However, if critical details such as patient outcomes were missing, this limitation was noted as “not available.” If no specific information about the salicylate poisoning could be obtained from an article or from the prior reviews, we excluded the article from our review. We also excluded five case reports due to lack of availability of the paper or incomplete details such as salicylate blood levels and case data. – From each case report, we recorded the year of publication, patient age, sex, concentration of topical salicylate/vehicle, peak reported salicylate concentration (mg/dL), day of peak plasma levels, underlying diseases, case outcome, and physical exam findings. If available, we noted body weight, salicylate concentration, diluent, estimated surface exposure, length of exposure, and timing of administration. All salicylate units were converted into mg/dL for consistency. Intact skin was defined as having no compromised skin integrity secondary to underlying dermatological conditions. This expanded the total reported cases to 44, including the current case presented here ( ). The first review published in 1996 reviewed 17 cases. Two cases had no reported ages. The lowest plasma concentration reported was 14.0 mg/dL, and the highest was 223.0 mg/dL. , Two cases did not have recorded plasma concentrations, and one was sampled postmortem. , The most common symptoms of salicylate poisoning noted included tachypnea (32.5%), vomiting (25.5%), nausea (21.0%), and tinnitus (21.0%). Seven cases involved toxicities with intact skin. , , , , , , Death occurred in five cases (11.6%). Death was observed in patients with psoriasis and tinea imbricata, and there was one isolated death reported in a patient with intact skin. , , The final outcome of seven cases was not available. , , , , , DISCUSSION Our case report exemplifies the rare but important instance of systemic salicylate toxicity resulting from topical application of methyl salicylate over a large surface area in an elderly patient with multiple comorbidities. Because he applied the topical salicylates on himself, the amount that he may have ingested intentionally or accidentally is unknown. Since the last published reviews on topical salicylate poisonings, 13 cases have been added with 12 new cases reported from the literature and one case reported here. , Despite reduced use of topical salicylate in dermatology, cases of topical salicylate toxicity continue to be reported. When informed of the blood salicylate levels, the family disclosed that the patient had recently been using a popular, aggressively marketed, methyl salicylate-containing cream with multiple applications to about 18% of his body surface area within a two-day period. Notably, despite intact skin and near-normal renal function, the patient had significant absorption of salicylate and a prolonged salicylate half-life resulting in toxicity. In a voluntary study involving human subjects, the half-life after complete absorption of dermal salicylate was obtained from plasma concentrations. Subjects wore from 2–8 adhesive patches impregnated with methyl salicylate. The harmonic mean terminal half-life of methyl salicylate was determined to be 3.0 ± 1.2 hours. The half-life of methyl salicylate in our case report was prolonged and suggests continued absorption, additional oral exposure, or chronic salicylate exposure. In cases where data were available, as in the case presented here, toxicities typically manifested within a few days of topical salicylate use. Severe toxicities, including seizures, severe metabolic acidosis, cerebral edema, acute respiratory distress syndrome, hypoglycemia, hypoglycorrhachia, ketosis, and death, were most often linked to applications of high-concentration salicylate products involving large body surface areas over extended periods. Elevated and toxic doses of salicylate typically occur with blood levels above 20–30 mg/dL, and can disrupt key physiological processes, leading to a wide range of harmful effects. Elevated toxic salicylate levels can impair oxidative phosphorylation, resulting in adenosine triphosphate production failure while also increasing oxygen consumption, metabolic acidosis, and heat generation. Clinical manifestations in early toxicity often occur from stimulation of the brain’s respiratory center causing initial tachypnea and respiratory alkalosis, as seen in this case. The inhibition of Krebs cycle enzymes reduces glucose availability systemically and in the brain. This promotes organic acid accumulation, which leads to metabolic acidosis. Resultant significant fluid and electrolyte losses lead to dehydration, sodium and potassium depletion, and reduced buffering capacity. Once absorbed, salicylic acid is metabolized by the liver to more water-soluble byproducts. In considering topical dosing, the surface area treated, the concentration of salicylate used should not be excessive; the use of occlusive dressings, the frequency of application, and the patient’s underlying volume- and renal-status must be considered. A study with patients with active psoriasis found that after 10 hours with occlusive dressing over the topical salicylates, 60% of the salicylate was absorbed. The priority in treating any poisoned patient is assessing the airway, oxygenation, and maintaining perfusion of organs. Once toxicity is identified, it is critical to lower the salicylate levels. Resuscitation should begin with thorough skin decontamination with soap and water to remove any remaining drug and fluids, and dextrose 5% with 3 ampules of sodium bicarbonate to buffer the metabolic acidosis; added potassium chloride increases renal excretion and

underlying volume- and renal-status must be considered. A study with patients with active psoriasis found that after 10 hours with occlusive dressing over the topical salicylates, 60% of the salicylate was absorbed. The priority in treating any poisoned patient is assessing the airway, oxygenation, and maintaining perfusion of organs. Once toxicity is identified, it is critical to lower the salicylate levels. Resuscitation should begin with thorough skin decontamination with soap and water to remove any remaining drug and fluids, and dextrose 5% with 3 ampules of sodium bicarbonate to buffer the metabolic acidosis; added potassium chloride increases renal excretion and helps to prevent brain absorption by ion trapping of the salicylate. Potassium chloride is often added to prevent hypokalemia, the presence of which will inhibit alkalinization of the urine. Hemodialysis is indicated for severe acidosis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, severe altered mental status, seizures, kidney failure, refractory hypotension, and salicylate levels greater than 100 mg/dL for acute exposures and potentially lower levels for chronic exposure. The Extracorporeal Treatments in Poisoning workgroup recommendations and indications for salicylate poisoning are very useful. In addition to the concentration and surface area of application, different formulations of topical salicylic acid have different levels of systemic absorption. A study by Morra et al found that the methyl salicylate used in the current case demonstrated higher absorption compared to other formulations such as trolamine salicylate. Methyl salicylate reached detectable serum salicylate levels within one hour of application with cumulative absorption increasing after repeated applications. In contrast, trolamine salicylate showed minimal skin absorption, with serum salicylate levels often undetectable and significantly lower recovery in urine. Our review of 43 previous cases plus the current case of topical salicylate toxicity corroborates this observation. As summarized in , symptoms of topical salicylate toxicity are broad and generally develop within a few days of use, particularly when applied over large body surface areas, compromised skin, or with repeated applications. While the most common findings in the literature review were metabolic abnormalities, altered mental status, tachypnea, vomiting, nausea, and tinnitus, the current patient had altered mental status, metabolic acidosis with elevated anion gap, and tachypnea (with respiratory alkalemia) but only reported tinnitus after he regained his baseline mental status and the salicylate levels had fallen. This suggests that older patients or those with comorbid conditions like dementia can be a challenge to diagnose and demonstrates the need for heightened clinical suspicion when presented with a limited history and symptoms. This case report and descriptive analysis of similar historical cases emphasizes the need for further patient education about the potential toxicity of OTC topical salicylates and their use to improve their safety among the general population and particularly in vulnerable populations such as children, renal-compromised patients, and patients with baseline altered mental status. This report reinforces the need for clinicians to suspect and inquire about topical salicylate use in patients with an elevated anion gap and altered mental status given its widespread use and availability. LIMITATIONS Retrospective literature research has several limitations. Some older publications, particularly those predating digital archiving, may have been excluded in the search due to their limited availability and not being included in the electronic databases searched. A few publications were not available. If available, abstracts were used, but some provided limited data such as patient outcomes, sex, age, and symptoms. Publication bias clearly favors publication of toxic cases but considering the limited number of cases found over 72 years, the incidence of topical salicylate toxicity must be low. Case reports have significant limitations. This case report also has limitations in terms of history and potential chronic or oral dosing of salicylates that was denied by the family but still could have happened. CONCLUSION Topical salicylates have the potential for systemic toxicity particularly when large doses of methyl salicylate are applied in high concentrations in vulnerable populations such as patients with compromised renal function, and in pediatric patients with a large surface-to-body ratio. The inappropriate use of methyl salicylate products in particular, especially in high concentrations over large body surface areas, on compromised skin, and with repeated applications can pose significant health risks. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for salicylate toxicity in patients presenting with non-specific symptoms such as altered mental status, or unexplained metabolic acidosis or tachypnea especially in those with a history of topical salicylate use. Although salicylate toxicity is not common, early recognition and intervention are essential to prevent or reduce clinical toxicity and ensure rapid resolution. Widespread patient education about the toxicological risk of these heavily advertised topical salicylate products is also needed.

chunks.content: 1. Introduction Poisoning constitutes a critical global public health challenge, necessitating prompt intervention to optimize clinical outcomes. Extracorporeal treatments (ECTRs), including hemodialysis and hemoperfusion, play a pivotal role in enhancing toxin clearance. [ – ] In cases of inadequate antidotes, low toxin protein binding, or multi-organ dysfunction, urgent femoral venous catheter insertion is often indispensable to facilitate rapid extracorporeal therapy. [ ] Femoral access is preferred for its high procedural success rate and expeditious placement. [ , ] However, catheter-related thrombosis (CRT) following insertion presents significant clinical challenges, particularly concerning safe catheter removal. While CRT is a recognized complication of vascular access, its implications in poisoned patients: who frequently exhibit acute, complex conditions with potential toxin-induced coagulation disorders or hemolysis [ ] (remain underinvestigated). In non-poisoned populations, especially those with long-term vascular access needs (e.g., oncology, chronic kidney disease, critical illness), CRT is well-documented, with reported incidences of 15% to 60% for central venous CRT. Femoral vein catheters carry elevated risks due to anatomical factors (proximity to inguinal crease, increased mechanical stress) and longer dwell times. [ ] Key risk factors include catheter characteristics (large diameter, multi-lumen), indwelling duration > 72 hours, patient-specific attributes (age > 60 years, obesity, thrombophilia, immobility), and comorbidities (cancer, sepsis, coagulation disorders). [ ] In case of clinical suspicion, the initial diagnostic approach for CRT is represented by duplex ultrasound (DUS). Clinical guidelines for the treatment of CRT advocate low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), and delayed catheter removal for large/symptomatic thrombi to mitigate pulmonary embolism (PE) risk. [ ] However, these strategies are tailored to chronic conditions and may not directly apply to poisoned patients, who typically require short-term ECTR (median duration < 72 hours) and exhibit distinct pathophysiology, including toxin-induced hyperfibrinogenemia, D-dimer elevation, and transient hemodynamic instability: factors that may alter thrombotic risk profiles and management priorities. Existing literature on CRT predominantly focuses on chronic disease or long-term access populations, creating a significant evidence gap for the short-term ECTR context in poisoning care. [ – ] Critical uncertainties include the association between CRT and PE/deep vein thrombosis (DVT) risk during catheter removal, and the influence of demographic, clinical, or laboratory factors on CRT development in this population. [ , ] Current CRT management guidelines lack specificity for poisoned patients, whose toxin-mediated hematological abnormalities and short-treatment durations may modulate thrombotic risks. [ , , ] And there is no recognized or high-level evidence to support that CRT is a contraindication for direct femoral venous catheter removal. [ ] We can make the following hypotheses: CRT may not significantly increase the risk of catheter removal; maybe there are certain predictors for the progression of CRT; since coagulation abnormalities in poisoned patients mostly improve with toxin clearance and alleviation of the patient’s condition, CRT may not require long-term anticoagulation. This retrospective study aims to address these knowledge gaps by systematically evaluating: incidence of CRT in poisoned patients with femoral venous catheters; associated demographic, clinical, and laboratory risk factors; thrombosis-related complications; and the role of anticoagulation in thrombus resolution/recanalization. [ , ] By characterizing these factors, the study seeks to inform evidence-based strategies for safe femoral venous catheter removal in poisoned patients with CRT, improving management of this under-researched complication. 2. Methods 2.1. Study design and patients selection A retrospective cohort study was conducted at the Department of Poisoning Medicine and Critical Care of the First Affiliated Hospital of Chongqing Medical and Pharmaceutical College, including patients admitted between August 01, 2020 and August 31, 2024. Eligibility criteria included: age 15 to 80 years; confirmed poisoning via exposure history, clinical manifestations, and laboratory/imaging findings; femoral venous catheterization for ECTRs; lower extremity DUS performed; and ECTR indication based on toxin-specific risk assessment per established guidelines. Exclusion criteria were: missing post-removal DUS before discharge; incomplete laboratory data; non-femoral venous access for ECTRs; bilateral femoral catheterization; anticoagulation use between ECTR completion and catheter removal; or thrombolysis/interventional procedures before removal. Patients were classified into CRT and non-CRT groups based on DUS findings. 2.2. Treatments Femoral venous catheterization (12Fr-20 cm double-lumen catheter, Zhengzhou Di’ao, China) was performed under ultrasound guidance by critical care physicians after informed consent. ECTR modality (e.g., hemodialysis, hemoperfusion) was selected based on toxin characteristics. The implementation of ECTRs was comprehensively determined based on current guidelines [ , ] and individual patient assessments, including toxin characteristics (such as molecular weight, protein binding rate, elimination half-life), clinical severity (such as altered consciousness, hemodynamic instability), and evidence of end-organ dysfunction (such as acute kidney injury, respiratory failure). Clinical data included catheter indwelling time (hours), total ECTR duration (hours), and catheter dysfunction (resolved by catheter replacement if needed). When removing catheters in patients with confirmed CRT, the strategy adhered to current guidelines on the management of CRT and DVT, the indications for continued catheter retention and catheter removal are evaluated. When removing catheters in patients with confirmed CRT, the strategy adhered to current guidelines on the management of CRT and DVT, the indications for continued catheter retention and catheter removal are evaluated. Post-ECTR catheter removal involved 15-minute pressure bandaging at the puncture site. Routine DUS was conducted within 48 hours of removal to assess thrombus status. In the CRT group, anticoagulation strategies were recorded, including dose adjustments for liver/kidney dysfunction [ ] ; anticoagulants were categorized as LMWH alone, LMWH bridged with rivaroxaban, or no anticoagulation, with hospitalization duration of anticoagulation (days) and pre-discharge DUS results documented. 2.3. Laboratory and ultrasound assessments Pre-insertion baseline laboratory values, including complete blood count and toxin-specific analyses, were collected. Sonologist performed DUS evaluated thrombus status in the distal external iliac, common femoral, and distal deep veins, classified into: complete recanalization (no thrombus; partial recanalization) thrombus size reduced ≥ 50% or stable; thrombosis progression: enlarged thrombus or new adjacent DVT. Two DUS results were collected, including the 1st examination around the time of catheter removal and the last examination before hospital discharge; PE suspicion prompted computed tomography angiography. 2.4. Statistical analysis Statistical analysis was performed using Statistic Package for Social Science 26.0 (International Business Machines Corporation, Armonk ). Statistical significance was defined as P < .05. Continuous variables with normal distribution were reported as mean ± standard deviation, while those with skewed distribution use median (interquartile range). Student t test or the Mann–Whitney rank sum test according to the normality of their distribution. Categorical variables were expressed as frequency and percentage. Categorical variables were compared using the χ 2 test (or Fisher exact test for variables with an expected value of < 5). Significant variables in the hypothesis testing were entered into a multivariate logistic regression model to identify independent predictors. Goodness-of-fit of the regression model was examined with the Hosmer–Lemeshow test, of which P < .05 was considered statistically significant. Associations were expressed as OR with 95% CI. 3. Results 3.1. Patient characteristics After reviewing the medical records of discharged patients, of 171 patients who received ECTRs for poisoning, 71 met the inclusion criteria (Fig. ). Of patients that received a DUS, 38% had CRT. As can be seen in Table , there were no significant differences in most demographic characteristics and laboratory test results between patients with (n = 27) or without (n = 44) CRT. However, fibrinogen (3.23 (IQR = 0.83) g/L) and D-dimer (1.16 (IQR = 1.61) mg/L) concentrations were significantly higher in the CRT group ( P < .001). Also, the positive rate of D-dimer (n = 20 (74.1%)) was much higher in the CRT group ( P < .001). 3.2. Types of poisons Details of the types of poisons in the 2 groups of patients are shown in Table . Regarding the relative frequenices of the poison types, no significant differences were found between the 2 groups ( P > .05). 3.3. Clinical data The clinical data of the 2 groups of patients are shown in Table . There was no significant difference in femoral venous catheterization side ( P = .477), indwelling catheter time ( P = .140), total time of ECTRs ( P = .962), or catheter dysfunction ( P = .349) between the 2 groups. But the incidence of local symptoms was significantly higher in the CRT group ( P < 0.001). No puncture site infections occurred in either group. In terms of complications, although the incidence of progressive lower extremity DVT was higher in the CRT group ( P = .051), no major bleeding events or typical PE symptoms were observed in either group, including shortness of breath, chest pain, hemoptysis, jugular vein filling, or hypotension. No deaths were directly caused by catheter removal or its complications. 3.4. Statistical analysis for indicators of the CRT group In the multivariate logistic regression model (Table ), independent indicators of poisoned patients included positive D-dimer ( P = .002) and local symptoms ( P = .002). The Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test indicated a good model fit ( P = .540). The receiver operating characteristic curve indicated that the area under the curve for the combined prediction of CRT by fibrinogen, positive D-dimer, and local symptoms was 0.840 (95% CI: 0.736–0.924) (Fig. ). 3.5. Data description of the CRT group According to the DUS findings in the CRT group, thrombus outcomes post-catheter removal included complete recanalization in 22/27 (81.5%) patients (defined as no residual thrombus on post-removal DUS),

The receiver operating characteristic curve indicated that the area under the curve for the combined prediction of CRT by fibrinogen, positive D-dimer, and local symptoms was 0.840 (95% CI: 0.736–0.924) (Fig. ). 3.5. Data description of the CRT group According to the DUS findings in the CRT group, thrombus outcomes post-catheter removal included complete recanalization in 22/27 (81.5%) patients (defined as no residual thrombus on post-removal DUS), partial recanalization/stability in 4/27 (14.8%) patients (with thrombus size unchanged or reduced without complete resolution), and thrombosis progression in 1/27 (3.7%) patients (characterized by increased thrombus volume or new distal DVT). No cases of PE were observed across any thrombus outcome category. Since this study excluded patients who received anticoagulant therapy for CRT between the end of ECTR and catheter removal, the anticoagulant therapies analyzed in the results were all interventions administered for CRT after catheter removal. The distribution of anticoagulants was as follows: LMWH in 17/27 (63.0%) patients, LMWH bridged with rivaroxaban in 6/27 (22.2%) patients, and no anticoagulation in 4/27 (14.8%) patients. Some poisoned patients had abnormal liver and kidney function in the early stages, but all improved after ECTRs. The doses of anticoagulant treatment were all determined according to the usual anticoagulation standards. In the CRT group, 4/27 (14.8%) patients did not receive anticoagulation therapy, 17/27 (63.0%) patients received anticoagulation therapy for 1 to 10 days (5.53 ± 2.94 days), and 6/27 (22.2%) patients received anticoagulation therapy for 11 to 35 days (22.17 ± 7.99 days). None of the discharged patients experienced progression of CRT to extensive DVT after discontinuing anticoagulation. 4. Discussion This retrospective study compared poisoned patients with femoral venous catheters for ECTR, identifying 2 key findings in CRT versus non-CRT groups. First, CRT did not pose immediate life-threatening risk during short-term removal: DUS showed high post-removal thrombus recanalization, supporting safe immediate removal without delay. These outcomes suggest CRT alone does not require delayed removal in acute poisoning. Second, elevated fibrinogen, positive D-dimer, and local puncture-site symptoms correlated with higher CRT risk, indicating targeted screening via lower extremity venous ultrasonography to monitor progression. Poisoning is a unique clinical condition marked by rapid progression, multisystem toxin effects, internal environment disruption, and the need for time-critical ECTRs: both short-term interventions. While some toxins affect coagulation, the direct link between specific toxins and thrombosis remains unclear. Extracorporeal treatments (ECTRs), including hemodialysis and hemoperfusion, play a pivotal role in enhancing toxin clearance. [ – ] In cases of inadequate antidotes, low toxin protein binding, or multi-organ dysfunction, urgent femoral venous catheter insertion is often indispensable to facilitate rapid extracorporeal therapy. [ ] Femoral access is preferred for its high procedural success rate and expeditious placement. [ , ] However, catheter-related thrombosis (CRT) following insertion presents significant clinical challenges, particularly concerning safe catheter removal. [ ] In case of clinical suspicion, the initial diagnostic approach for CRT is represented by duplex ultrasound (DUS). Clinical guidelines for the treatment of CRT advocate low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), and delayed catheter removal for large/symptomatic thrombi to mitigate pulmonary embolism (PE) risk. Existing literature on CRT predominantly focuses on chronic disease or long-term access populations, creating a significant evidence gap for the short-term ECTR context in poisoning care. [ ] We can make the following hypotheses: CRT may not significantly increase the risk of catheter removal; maybe there are certain predictors for the progression of CRT; since coagulation abnormalities in poisoned patients mostly improve with toxin clearance and alleviation of the patient’s condition, CRT may not require long-term anticoagulation. This retrospective study aims to address these knowledge gaps by systematically evaluating: incidence of CRT in poisoned patients with femoral venous catheters; associated demographic, clinical, and laboratory risk factors; thrombosis-related complications; and the role of anticoagulation in thrombus resolution/recanalization. documents.title: EXTRIP recommendations for extracorporeal treatment of metformin poisoning

chunks.content: Expanding the evidence for managing metformin poisoning to support decision-making. Metformin-associated lactic acidosis is a well-described and commonly encountered condition associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Patients with metformin-associated lactic acidosis are frequently managed in the intensive care unit with supportive care, including volume resuscitation and consideration of an extracorporeal treatment to correct metabolic acidemia and remove metformin and lactate. The Extracorporeal Treatments in Poisoning Workgroup published evidence-based consensus recommendations in 2015 regarding the use of extracorporeal treatment in metformin toxicity. These recommendations list both clinical and biochemical indications, and they outline the rationale and evidence supporting each recommendation. Subsequent publications have provided new information regarding metformin-associated lactic acidosis and its treatment. A retrospective study showed that patients who did not meet the Extracorporeal Treatments in Poisoning Workgroup criteria for initiation of an extracorporeal treatment had a 100% survival. In patients who met the criteria, survival was approximately 75%; only 66% of these patients received an extracorporeal treatment, and this treatment did not appear to impact survival. Two other retrospective studies in patients diagnosed with metformin-associated lactic acidosis noted that extracorporeal treatments did not improve survival. However, those who received an extracorporeal treatment were more severely ill, potentially supporting a benefit from this intervention. A systematic review of patients receiving continuous kidney replacement therapy identified an overall survival that was higher than the overall survival in patients included in the Workgroup publication. This led the authors to suggest that intermittent hemodialysis may not be the preferred treatment for metformin toxicity. However, a closer look at the Workgroup data identified improved survival with each decade since the initial reports in the 1970s. Furthermore, there are multiple reports of persistent metformin-associated lactic acidosis that did not improve with standard continuous kidney replacement therapy, prompting an increase in the dosage of the extracorporeal treatment. The data supporting these observations are largely derived from retrospective studies, which have inherent biases, so prospective studies are required. Case-based decision-making is always necessary, but in general, we continue to follow the Extracorporeal Treatments in Poisoning Workgroup criteria because a convincing reason for changing these has not yet been presented. This includes the use of intermittent hemodialysis where possible, particularly in cases of severe poisoning. For patients with less severe poisoning or when intermittent hemodialysis is not readily available, it is reasonable to trial continuous modalities with careful observation for deterioration.
